'''Harbor Point''' is a redevelopment located in the [[South End of Stamford|South End]] of [[Stamford, Connecticut]], United States, in southwestern [[Fairfield County, Connecticut|Fairfield County]]. Harbor Point is a transit-oriented,{{Citation needed|date=June 2022}} [[mixed-use development]] near the [[Stamford Transportation Center]] on [[Long Island Sound]], which includes approximately 2,750 new housing units as of January 2021, with plans for 4,000 total units.<ref name=":0" /> The development also includes office buildings,<ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Siwolop |first=Sana |date=2010-12-07 |title=Sprawling Development in Stamford Is Filling Out |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/08/realestate/commercial/08harbor.html |url-status=live |access-date=2022-06-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150928184421/https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/08/realestate/commercial/08harbor.html |archive-date=2015-09-28 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> restaurants,<ref name=":3" /> parks,<ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last=Prevost |first=Lisa |date=2022-01-12 |title=The South End of Stamford, Conn.: Master-Planned With Luxury Rentals, and Lots of Pets |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/01/12/realestate/living-stamford-ct-south-end.html |access-date=2022-06-18 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and a [[boardwalk]].<ref name=":4" />

[[File:Harbor Point seen from plane en route to HPN airport.jpg|thumb|Harbor Point aerial view]]

It is made up of five distinct areas, each centered on a park or waterfront feature.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022}} The ''[[Stamford Advocate]]'' has called it "reportedly one of the largest redevelopment projects in the nation" and "the city’s fastest-changing neighborhood".<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Carella |first=Angela |date=2018-01-12 |title=Stamford's Harbor Point: City seeks to discern South End changes |url=https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/local/article/Stamford-s-Harbor-Point-City-seeks-to-discern-12493895.php |access-date=2022-03-21 |website= |publisher=[[Stamford Advocate]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

While the redevelopment has drawn praise from many in the city for revitalizing what was once a declining industrial neighborhood, a number of South End residents have raised concerns about its displacement of long-time residents and smaller businesses, large property acquisitions by developers, and the proliferation of short-term residents characteristic of [[gentrification]].<ref name=":0" />

== History ==
The area of contemporary Harbor Point was historically used for industrial purposes, dominated by the [[Yale (company)|Yale & Towne]] Lock Works, which first located to the area in 1868.<ref name="KerschusHerzan">Nils Kerschus and John Herzan (August, 1985). "{{NRHP url|id=86000472|title=National Register of Historic Places Inventory-Nomination: South End Historic District}}". National Park Service.</ref> The company's presence fueled the area's economic growth, and by the 1890s, the Yale & Towne Lock Works had grown so large that it dominated the economy of Stamford at one point employing nearly 25% of the Stamford population.<ref name="KerschusHerzan" /> It would hold this position for over fifty years, during which time the city would be known as the "Lock City."<ref name="KerschusHerzan" />

Beginning in 2005, Antares Investment Partners began acquiring an array of properties in the South End of Stamford, and announced plans to redevelop an {{Convert|80|acre|ha}} portion of the neighborhood as part of a project called Harbor Point.<ref name=":3" /> The project, which one [[The New York Times|New York Times]] article called "one of the largest and most ambitious redevelopment efforts in the country", was sold to [[Norwalk, Connecticut|Norwalk]]-based Building and Land Technology (BLT), a private development company, in September 2008.<ref name=":3" />

By 2010, BLT saw residential growth which "exceeded" the company's expectations, but experienced more difficulty in attracting tenants for the redevelopment's office facilities.<ref name=":3" /> Connecticut's first [[Fairway Market]], a [[New York metropolitan area|New York metro area]] supermarket chain, opened its seventh and largest store—an {{convert|85000|sqft|m2|adj=on}} store at Market and Canal streets in Harbor Point in November 2010.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Kim |first=Elizabeth |date=2010-10-20 |title=New Fairway store signals area's revival |url=https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/news/article/With-Fairway-South-End-set-to-become-Fairfield-716042.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160804112646/https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/news/article/With-Fairway-South-End-set-to-become-Fairfield-716042.php |archive-date=2016-08-04 |access-date=2022-03-21 |publisher=[[Stamford Advocate]]}}</ref> The Fairway Market was the first retailer to open in Harbor Point as part of the redevelopment.<ref name=":1" /> Throughout subsequent years, Harbor Point continued to see rapid residential growth, mostly due to an influx of higher-income individuals.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" />

The Fairway Market was closed in August 2020, resulting in 109 layoffs.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schott |first1=Paul |date=2020-08-20 |title=Fairwell: After months of going-staying notices, Stamford Fairway is gone |publisher=Stamford Advocate |url=https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/business/article/Fairwell-After-months-of-going-staying-notices-15497908.php |accessdate=1 October 2020}}</ref> As of January 2022, no new tenants have moved into the building, which has been used as a [[COVID-19 testing]] site during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Del Valle |first=Verónica |date=2022-01-06 |title=Stamford launches new PCR COVID-19 testing site at former Fairway building |url=https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/news/coronavirus/article/Stamford-launches-new-PCR-COVID-19-testing-site-16755188.php |access-date=2022-03-21 |publisher=[[Stamford Advocate]]}}</ref>

In April 2022, the Lofts at Yale & Towne, an apartment building converted from an old Yale & Towne factory which was one of the redevelopment's first projects, was ordered by the city government to be demolished after it was found to be tilting and sinking after its foundation was found to be unsound.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-06 |title='A Disaster,' Says Architect, As Owner Moves to Demolish 225-Unit Lofts at Yale & Towne |url=https://ctexaminer.com/2022/04/06/a-disaster-says-architect-as-owner-moves-to-demolish-225-unit-lofts-at-yale-towne/ |access-date=2022-06-18 |website=The Connecticut Examiner |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Historic district ==
{{Main|South End of Stamford}}
The [[South End Historic District (Connecticut)|South End Historic District]] covers a {{convert|177.1|acre|adj=on}} area of the South End neighborhood including many areas in Harbor Point. The district includes 449 buildings, most dating from the 1870s to the 1930s, and also "an early naturalistic cemetery, and an iron bridge." Other notable buildings are Number 715 on Atlantic Street, a tenement building, and the Holy Name Rectory. The historic district includes the Pulaski Street Bridge, a wrought-iron lenticular through-truss bridge over the [[Rippowam River]].<ref name="KerschusHerzan" />

== Reception ==
The redevelopment of Harbor Point in the 21st century has drawn mixed reactions. Some have praised the project for bringing economic growth to a once economically disadvantaged part of [[Stamford, Connecticut|Stamford]],<ref name=":0" /> whereas others have disputed the economic impact on the local community,<ref name=":0" /> and have raised concerns about the quick pace of development and the affordability of the new housing built in the area.<ref name=":0" />

A 2018 article in the Westchester & Fairfield County Business Journals praised the Harbor Point redevelopment for turning an area once "marked by pollution and high crime rates" into an environmentally-friendly [[transit-oriented development]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Zimmerman |first=Kevin |date=2018-12-23 |title=Stamford's Harbor Point at 10 years: Thumbs up from most stakeholders |url=https://westfaironline.com/109639/stamfords-harbor-point-at-10-thumbs-up-from-most-stakeholders/ |access-date=2022-03-21 |website=Westfair Communications |language=en-US}}</ref> The COO of BLT, the main developer of the initial development known as Harbor Point, said that the initial project brought in 30 restaurants and created thousands of jobs.<ref name=":2" /> The company has also highlighted the tax revenue the project has earned the city.<ref name=":2" />

A number of local homeowners have raised concerns about the frenzied pace at which developers, led by the area's main developer, BLT, acquired properties.<ref name=":0" /> Others took issue with frequent attempts by BLT and other developers to purchase their own properties, as well as the allegedly low prices they offered.<ref name=":0" />

Another concern raised by local residents is that most housing built as part of the redevelopment can only be rented, instead of bought outright.<ref name=":0" /> According to a January 2018 article by the ''[[Stamford Advocate]]'', the average rent for a one bedroom apartment in Harbor Point is about $2,000 per month,<ref name=":0" /> and a January 2022 piece by ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported that the average one bedroom rent was $2,568.<ref name=":4" /> Units designated as "affordable" by Harbor Point's main developer, BLT, went for an average of roughly $1,200 as of January 2018, which some local residents have described as out of reach.<ref name=":0" />

Some long-time residents have lamented the number of short-term residents the redevelopment has brought, and suggested that the redevelopment's focus on rental units has not created a large amount of jobs in the area.<ref name=":0" /> Concerns over the preservation of nearby existing structures has also been raised by some locals, who have proposed designating the area as a local historic district.<ref name=":4" /> In 2020, BLT took down part of a vacant factory on the National Register of Historic Places dating from the late 19th century.<ref name=":4" /> Residents of the redevelopment have hit back against claims that they're "not part of the community", saying that the area's recent changes have resulted in sizable economic growth. Some have also disputed claims of high turnover within the redeveloped units.<ref name=":0" /> Some residents of Harbor Point have raised concerns about crime and street lighting in the surrounding areas.<ref name=":0" />

In addition, some building sites have been picketed by labor unions over alleged violations and unfair practices.<ref name=":2" />

Environmental group [[Soundkeeper]] sued the Stamford Zoning Board for what it charged was a violation of legally required compliances with environmental, coastal management and local zoning laws.<ref name=":2" /> The case was dismissed in October 2018 by a state Superior Court judge.<ref name=":2" />
